notes: Ruling slot 23 = House of Grimaldi (Rainier III). The UND, which won all 18 National Council seats in 1968, stays in MD slot 0 because MD's Rassemblement & Enjeux is the same organisation renamed (slot 0 has starting popularity); its MD icon is generic, so icon and wiki are null. Slot 1 = Diocese of Monaco (state religion), slot 13 = the French-run Princely Government, slot 14 = Comité National des Traditions Monégasques, slot 4 = MUD (communist-union alliance), slot 18 = USM. Other slots are catchy factions rooted in real Riviera milieus, since Monaco had almost no other organised politics in 1970.

0.name: Union Nationale et Démocratique
0.text:
The National and Democratic Union was formed in 1962 by the merger of the National Union of Independents and the National Democratic Entente, the two lists of Monegasque notables that dominated the National Council. In March 1968 it won all eighteen seats, and its leader Auguste Médecin was elected President of the Council. Only Monegasque citizens, a few thousand people, may vote.

The UND is the establishment party of the principality: loyal to Prince Rainier and to the 1962 constitution, which leaves executive power with the Prince and his government while the Council votes laws and the budget. It defends priority for Monegasques in jobs and housing, the absence of income tax and Rainier's ambitious land reclamation. Its leverage lies in its monopoly on the Council.

1.name: Diocèse de Monaco
1.text:
The Diocese of Monaco was created in 1887 and answers directly to the Holy See. Roman Catholicism is the state religion under the constitution, and the Cathedral of Saint Nicholas, where Prince Rainier married Grace Kelly in 1956, is the spiritual centre of a principality whose native families remain devout.

The Church defends Christian marriage, Catholic schooling and public morality in a state that lives from a casino, a contradiction it manages with discretion: Monegasque citizens themselves are barred from the gaming rooms. It supports the Prince and the established order, preaches charity towards the immigrant workers who build the new Monaco and applies the reforms of the Second Vatican Council with caution. Its leverage is moral and ceremonial, but deeply rooted.

2.name: Les Parlementaristes
2.text:
The Parliamentarians are the liberal-minded Monegasques, lawyers, doctors, teachers and younger civil servants, who want the National Council to be more than a chamber of notables. They remember January 1959, when Prince Rainier suspended the constitution and sent the Council home after a budget dispute, and they regard the constitution of 1962 as a beginning rather than an end.

They seek a Council with real budgetary control and the right to initiate laws, a government answerable to the elected deputies, freedom of the press and open public debate. Pro-French and pro-European in outlook, they distrust both the Palace's paternalism and the UND's monopoly. Their weight is limited to salons and the professions, but they have the ear of younger voters.

3.name: Les Réformistes de la Condamine
3.text:
The Reformists of La Condamine are the moderate socialists of the port district: Monegasque and French employees of the casino company, municipal staff, teachers and craftsmen who want social progress without communist leadership. Many belong to the unions of the USM but reject the Democratic Union Movement's alliance with the communists, and they follow with interest the new French Socialist Party founded in 1969.

They call for social housing for Monegasque families and for the workers who serve the principality, pensions and wages that keep pace with France, and collective agreements in every sector. Loyal to the monarchy and to the Western alliance, they hope to give Monaco a respectable left that the Palace could accept. Their leverage is modest: a network of union delegates and municipal employees.

4.name: Mouvement d'Union Démocratique
4.text:
The Democratic Union Movement was founded in 1963 as an alliance of trade unionists and communists, the only organised opposition to the Monegasque establishment. It won one seat in 1963 but lost it in March 1968, when its list took about nine percent of the votes; its best-known candidate is the trade union leader Charles Soccal.

The MUD speaks for the workers of the casino company, the hotels and the building sites, and for the minority of Monegasque citizens who live from wages rather than rents. It demands higher pay, social housing, trade union rights and a more democratic constitution, and it is close to the communist left across the French border. Under the 1962 constitution its leverage lies in the unions rather than in the Council.

5.name: Les Enragés de la Condamine
5.text:
The Enragés of La Condamine are the young rebels of May 1968 in Monaco: pupils of the Lycée Albert Ier, apprentices and young hotel workers who joined the strikes and demonstrations that spread from France to the principality and won an across-the-board pay rise. Monaco has no university, so many now study at the new University of Nice, where they mix with anarchists and the Trotskyists of the Ligue communiste.

They mock the Palace, the casino and the jet set as a museum of privilege and call for self-management, sexual freedom and solidarity with Vietnam. They have no organisation beyond a few cafés, a duplicated news sheet and friendships across the border. Their leverage is the noise they make in a principality that prizes discretion above all.

6.name: Les Ultras du Rocher
6.text:
The Ultras of the Rock are the most conservative members of the old Monegasque families: retired officers, legitimist readers of the Action française press and Catholics dismayed by the liturgical reforms of the Second Vatican Council. They live in the narrow streets of Monaco-Ville and regard the high-rises, yachts and Hollywood glamour of the new Monte Carlo as a betrayal of the principality's soul.

They want a Prince who rules rather than reigns, free of the encumbrance of the 1962 constitution, and a Catholic, hierarchical state closed to modern permissiveness. They despise American mass culture and the financiers who arrived with Onassis, and they look to the authoritarian Catholic regimes of Spain and Portugal for inspiration. Their numbers are negligible, but their family names still count at court.

7.name: Les Rattachistes
7.text:
The Annexationists are a strand of opinion among French officials, Gaullist politicians of the Alpes-Maritimes and French residents of Monaco who see the principality as an anomaly: a tax shelter living off French services. They remember 1962, when General de Gaulle had customs posts set up on the border to force Monaco to tax French residents and companies, and they believe Paris settled for too little.

They favour strict French control through the Minister of State and the customs union, or outright integration into the French Republic, and admire the strong, sovereign state of the Fifth Republic, independent of Washington and NATO. Monegasques regard them as the principality's mortal danger. Their leverage lies in the French state, which holds the keys to Monaco's borders, water, electricity and defence.

8.name: Le Cercle de Yakymour
8.text:
The Yakymour Circle takes its name from the villa at Le Cannet where the Begum Om Habibeh, widow of Aga Khan III, keeps the memory of the late Imam. Around her and the young Aga Khan IV, a familiar figure of Riviera society like his father Prince Aly Khan before him, gathers a cosmopolitan circle of Ismaili notables, financiers and friends who frequent Monte Carlo's galas.

The Ismaili Imamat stands for a modern Shia Islam centred on education, health care, enterprise and loyalty to the countries where its followers live. It invests in schools, hospitals and businesses across East Africa and South Asia and shuns revolutionary politics. In Monaco its influence is social rather than political: discreet ties with the Palace, the bankers and the international set.

9.name: Hey'at-e Ashura
9.text:
The Ashura Circle is a handful of Iranian students at the University of Nice and Iranian employees of the Riviera's hotels who gather in a rented room for the mourning ceremonies of Muharram. Their preacher reads aloud the sermons and letters of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, exiled to Najaf since 1965, which reach them through Iranian student networks in Paris.

They hold that the Shah is a tyrant serving America and Israel, that the Iranian court's display of wealth on the Côte d'Azur insults a suffering people, and that society must be guided by the learned clergy. They despise the secular and Marxist Iranian opposition abroad and collect religious dues for Khomeini's representatives. In Monaco they have no influence at all; their loyalties lie with Najaf.

10.name: Majlis al-Riviera
10.text:
The Riviera Majlis is the informal court of Saudi and Gulf princes, ministers and financiers who summer on the Côte d'Azur, moor their yachts in Port Hercule and keep part of their fortunes with Monaco's banks. Around them gather agents, interpreters and a few Arab residents who arrange their affairs and serve as discreet links between the Palace and the oil monarchies of the Arabian peninsula.

Their Islam is that of the Saudi establishment and the Gulf dynasties: conservative, obedient to rulers and hostile to Nasserism, communism and revolutionary Islam alike. They admire Monaco as a fellow hereditary monarchy, value its discretion and invest in its property. Their leverage is money and prestige, and Rainier's government courts them as the oil wealth of the Gulf grows.

11.name: Ansar al-Khilafa
11.text:
The Partisans of the Caliphate are a cell of Jordanian, Palestinian and Tunisian students at the University of Nice, some of whom work summers in Monaco's hotels. They spread the ideas of Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Liberation Party founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by Taqi al-Din al-Nabhani and banned in most Arab states, meeting in student rooms and distributing duplicated pamphlets.

They teach that the defeat of 1967 proves the bankruptcy of Arab nationalism and that only a restored caliphate ruling by the sharia can unite the Muslims and liberate Palestine. Elections, socialism and Western capitalism are rejected as man-made systems, and Monaco's casino and luxury epitomise the decadence they denounce. Their influence is nil, but their discipline and secrecy are those of a revolutionary party.

12.name: Usrat al-Da'wa
12.text:
The Da'wa Family is a study circle of Moroccan, Tunisian and Algerian workers who labour on Monaco's building sites and in its hotel kitchens, joined by a few North African students from Nice. They pray in a room in Beausoleil and draw literature and visiting speakers from the Association of Islamic Students in France, founded in Paris in 1963 by the scholar Muhammad Hamidullah.

Inspired by the Muslim Brotherhood, the circle preaches an Islam that is complete, educated and socially engaged: prayer, moral discipline, mutual aid and the defence of Muslim dignity in Europe. It is hostile to both Arab socialism and Western permissiveness but seeks no confrontation with the authorities. Its leverage lies in the growing number of Muslim workers on whom Monaco's construction boom depends.

13.name: Gouvernement Princier
13.text:
The Princely Government exercises executive power in the Prince's name. It is headed by the Minister of State, by treaty a senior French official chosen by the Prince from candidates proposed by Paris, assisted by three Government Councillors for the interior, finance and public works. It is not answerable to the National Council, and many of its senior civil servants are seconded from the French administration.

The government embodies rule by administrators rather than politicians: it prepares laws and the budget, runs the land reclamation, housing and infrastructure programmes, and manages Monaco's delicate relationship with France. Cautious, technocratic and loyal to the Prince, it values order, prosperity and discretion over public debate. Its leverage lies in its control of the administration and the state's finances.

14.name: Comité National des Traditions Monégasques
14.text:
The National Committee for Monegasque Traditions was founded in 1924 by representatives of the old Monegasque families to preserve a national identity threatened by the flood of foreign residents. It runs the Museum of Old Monaco on the Rock, cultivates the Monegasque language, keeps alive the feast of Saint Devota and other religious festivals, and guards the memory of a people who are a small minority in their own country.

The committee is not a party, but it is the conscience of the native community: Catholic, monarchist, attached to the old town and dismayed by the towers and concrete of the new Monte Carlo. It wants priority for Monegasques, the teaching of their language and protection of their heritage,. Its leverage lies in the family networks it represents.

15.name: Société des Bains de Mer et du Cercle des Étrangers à Monaco
15.native_full: Société des Bains de Mer et du Cercle des Étrangers à Monaco
15.text:
The Sea Bathing Society, founded in 1863 under Prince Charles III, owns the Casino of Monte Carlo, the Hôtel de Paris, the Hermitage, the opera and much of the principality's prime property, and it is Monaco's largest employer. For years it was controlled by the Greek shipowner Aristotle Onassis, until in 1966 Prince Rainier had new state shares created, giving the government a majority and forcing Onassis to sell out.

The SBM is the pivot of Monaco's economy. It favours expansion into conference tourism, luxury hotels and seaside development to reduce its dependence on gambling, and it expects the state to protect its monopoly. Its leverage is enormous: whoever controls the SBM controls much of Monaco's revenue and employment.
15.wiki: Société des bains de mer de Monaco

16.name: Les Commerçants de la Condamine
16.text:
The Traders of La Condamine are the shopkeepers, restaurateurs, estate agents, small hoteliers and company directors whose prosperity depends on Monaco's freedom from income tax, abolished in 1869. They were shaken by the 1963 convention imposed by General de Gaulle after the crisis of 1962, which subjects recently arrived French residents to French taxation and taxes companies that earn more than a quarter of their turnover abroad.

They want as little regulation, red tape and taxation as possible, free rein for building and commerce, and a firm defence of Monaco's fiscal sovereignty against Paris. They resent the privileges of the SBM and the slow procedures of the Princely Government alike. Loyal to the Prince but impatient with bureaucracy, they draw their leverage from the commercial life of the principality.

17.name: Institut océanographique, Fondation Albert Ier, Prince de Monaco
17.native_full: Institut océanographique, Fondation Albert Ier, Prince de Monaco
17.text:
The Oceanographic Institute was founded in 1906 by Prince Albert I, the scientist-prince, and its spectacular museum on the cliffs of Monaco-Ville opened in 1910. Since 1957 it has been directed by Commander Jacques-Yves Cousteau, whose films and television series have made the undersea world famous across the globe.

In 1960 Cousteau and Prince Rainier led the outcry that forced France to abandon plans to dump radioactive waste into the Mediterranean, and the institute now warns of pollution, overfishing and the death of coastal waters. It stands for scientific research, protection of the seas and international cooperation above Cold War rivalry. Its leverage lies in Cousteau's fame and the Palace's patronage, which make Monaco a voice for the oceans.

18.name: Union des Syndicats de Monaco
18.text:
The Union of Monaco Trade Unions was founded on 6 October 1944, the day an ordinance authorised workers' unions after the Liberation, and was given the former Fascist headquarters, the Casa Italiana, as its home. It federates the unions of the casino, hotels, building trade, banks and public services, and its members include many French and Italian workers who cross the border each day.

The USM has won collective agreements, a supplementary pension scheme and, in the strikes of May 1968, a general pay rise, a social fund and housing benefits. It demands union rights for all, better wages and housing. Its leaders, among them Charles Soccal, also stand for the Democratic Union Movement, and its leverage lies in its power to paralyse the casino state.

19.name: Les Maos du Rocher
19.text:
The Maoists of the Rock are a handful of young Monegasques and French residents, students at Nice and young workers, who sell La Cause du peuple, the paper of the Gauche prolétarienne, at the gates of the building sites. They were shaped by May 1968 and by the cult of the Chinese Cultural Revolution among Paris students.

They follow Mao Zedong Thought, denounce the Soviet Union and the French Communist Party as revisionist and dream of a people's war against capitalism, of which Monaco, with its casino and tax exiles, is the perfect symbol. They seek to serve the people among immigrant labourers. Their numbers are tiny and the police watch them closely, but their slogans echo among young workers on both sides of the border.

20.name: Monaco aux Monégasques
20.text:
Monaco for the Monegasques is the cry of native citizens who feel swamped in their own country: they are a small minority of the residents, while foreigners, the French above all, fill the jobs, flats and businesses. It has no formal organisation, but its mood runs through neighbourhood associations, café talk and the UND's own back benches.

Its supporters demand absolute priority for Monegasques in employment, housing and public office, strict limits on naturalisation and residence permits, and an end to the influence of French officials over the principality's affairs. They suspect both the cosmopolitan rich and the immigrant workers of turning Monaco into a mere address. Their leverage lies in the votes of the citizen minority, which no politician on the Rock can ignore.

21.name: Les Soldats perdus
21.text:
The Lost Soldiers are veterans of the Algerian War and the OAS who settled on the Riviera after 1962 among the pied-noir repatriates of Nice, Menton and the hills above Monaco. Amnestied in 1968, they nurse the bitterness of defeat in veterans' bars and rifle clubs, and some find work as bodyguards and security men for the wealthy of Monte Carlo.

They despise de Gaulle's heirs, parliaments, communists and the 'traitors' who abandoned French Algeria, and dream of an authoritarian, nationalist order in France and Europe. Some are drawn to Ordre Nouveau, founded in Paris in November 1969 to unite the radical right. In Monaco they have no political standing, but their weapons skills and contacts make them a latent threat.

22.name: Compagnie des Carabiniers du Prince
22.text:
The Company of the Prince's Carabiniers, created in 1817, is the principality's only military unit: about a hundred men who guard the Prince's Palace, escort the sovereign family and perform the ceremonial changing of the guard that delights tourists. Under the 1918 treaty France guarantees Monaco's defence, so the Carabiniers, together with the fire brigade and the Public Security police, form the whole of the principality's armed strength.

The Carabiniers are a praetorian force devoted entirely to the Prince, many of them former soldiers of the French army, commanded by officers loyal to the Palace. They have no political tradition, but in a crisis they are the instrument through which the Prince could impose his will on the Rock, and their loyalty would decide any confrontation with the National Council.

23.name: Maison Grimaldi
23.text:
The House of Grimaldi has ruled Monaco since 1297. Prince Rainier III, on the throne since 1949, has transformed his small state: he married the American film star Grace Kelly in 1956, weathered General de Gaulle's blockade of 1962, granted the constitution of 1962 and in 1966 wrested control of the Sea Bathing Society from Aristotle Onassis. The succession rests with Hereditary Prince Albert, born in 1958, and his sisters Caroline and Stéphanie.

Under the 1962 constitution the Prince holds executive power, shares legislative power with the National Council and appoints the government, so the Palace remains the true centre of decision. Rainier pursues land reclamation, tourism, light industry and banking to secure Monaco's future, defends its sovereignty against Paris and courts American and international capital.
